research_question: What is the causal effect of contractions in bank credit supply on local real economic activity, particularly small business lending and employment, both during the 2008 financial crisis and in normal economic times?
data_description: The study combines several data sources at the county level in the United States. Small business loan originations are measured using Community Reinvestment Act lending data, allowing decomposition by lender. Pre-crisis bank market shares at the county level are used together with estimated bank-level supply shifts to construct predicted county-level lending shocks. Employment outcomes for small firms and overall employment come from the confidential Longitudinal Business Database, which provides establishment- and firm-level microdata covering U.S. businesses. The principal sample period spans 1997 through 2009, encompassing both a long pre-crisis window (1997–2007) used to assess normal-times effects and the crisis years 2007–2009. The unit of observation is the county-year.
institutional_context: The analysis is motivated by the sharp contraction in bank credit supply following the 2008 financial crisis, when many U.S. banks experienced funding and balance-sheet stresses that reduced their willingness or capacity to lend. Because small businesses tend to depend on relationship lending and face high costs of switching lenders, disruptions to specific banks can translate into localized credit constraints in the counties where those banks have a strong presence. Pre-crisis variation in which banks dominated different county lending markets, combined with heterogeneity in how individual banks adjusted their supply during the crisis, generated geographically uneven exposure to the credit shock. Comparing this crisis episode to the relatively tranquil 1997–2007 period provides a setting in which to examine whether bank-driven credit disruptions matter for local employment in normal times as well as in financial crises.

main_estimate.interpretation: 2SLS: 10% decline in small business lending → 1.75% decline in small-firm employment (midpoint of 0.15–0.20 range)

public_sources: CRA small business loan data (FFIEC, public, annual by bank-county)
proprietary_sources: Dun & Bradstreet employment by firm size (proprietary) — used for some specifications
data_availability.proxy_strategy: CRA + CBP + Call Reports are all public; main IV design fully replicable; D&B data can be proxied with CBP employment
data_availability.replicability: high — all core data sources publicly available from FFIEC and Census
data_availability.data_limitations: CRA data covers only banks above the reporting threshold (~$1B in assets, adjusted over time). Some county-level employment data may be suppressed for disclosure reasons. Constructing the shift-share instrument requires careful matching of banks to counties using CRA or Summary of Deposits data.
public_data_sources_detail: FFIEC CRA Disclosure Data (small business lending by bank-county — free)
FDIC Call Reports / FFIEC CDR (bank balance sheets, real estate exposure — free)
BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (county employment — free)

title: Do Credit Market Shocks Affect the Real Economy? Quasi-Experimental Evidence from the Great Recession and 'Normal' Economic Times
_note_on_journal: Previously listed as JF; actual publication is AEJ: Economic Policy. Retained because the IV design is exemplary for financial economics.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV — instrument = pre-crisis (2006) bank real estate loan exposure (real estate loans / total assets), interacted with the county-level distribution of bank lending; first stage: banks with higher real estate exposure cut small business lending more; exclusion restriction: pre-crisis real estate exposure affects current-period employment only through its effect on credit supply

key_variables.instrument: pre-2007 bank real estate loan share, weighted by pre-crisis bank market share in each county
key_variables.treatment: change in small business loan originations (CRA data), county-year
key_variables.outcome: change in employment at small firms (< 50 employees), county-year

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: A 10% decline in small business lending caused by supply-side bank shocks reduced small-firm employment by approximately 1.5–2%; effects concentrated in industries dependent on bank credit
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: Elasticity of employment to bank credit supply: ~0.15–0.20
key_robustness: placebo using large firm employment (less bank-dependent)

identification_strategy_detail.treatment: County-level change in small business lending
identification_strategy_detail.instrument: Pre-crisis bank-county lending shares interacted with each bank's real estate exposure (Bartik-style shift-share instrument)
identification_strategy_detail.endogenous_variable: Change in small business lending at county level
identification_strategy_detail.first_stage: Counties more exposed to banks with larger real estate losses experienced greater declines in small business lending
identification_strategy_detail.exclusion_restriction: Pre-crisis bank-county lending relationships combined with bank-level real estate exposure affect county employment only through the credit supply channel
identification_strategy_detail.sample_period: 2006-2010 for crisis period; extended sample for 'normal times' comparison

key_magnitudes.employment_elasticity: Significant negative employment effect per dollar decline in lending
key_magnitudes.crisis_vs_normal: Effect is concentrated during the crisis period; weak or absent during normal economic times

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.robustness_notes_detail: Robust to alternative measures of bank exposure, different employment outcomes, controlling for county-level demand shocks. 'Normal times' placebo shows weak effects, supporting the crisis-specific credit channel interpretation.
